summary: Defines the Bridging Control Protocol, a Network Control Protocol for the Point-to-Point Protocol. It lets two ends of a point-to-point link negotiate and then carry bridged frames, so the link can act as part of a bridged network. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Two networks can be joined by one long cable. This memo defines how the two ends of that cable agree to pass along whole network messages as a bridge, so both sides act like one network.

questions: how does ppp carry bridged ethernet frames
what is the ppp bridging control protocol protocol number
subtitle: How two ends of a PPP link negotiate to carry bridged LAN frames, so the link acts as part of a bridged network.

tldr.problem: Remote bridges need a standard way to join LANs across a point-to-point link, including spanning tree traffic, VLAN tags and LAN frame checksums, and PPP had no such agreement for bridging.
tldr.mechanism: The Bridging Control Protocol is a PPP Network Control Protocol that works like LCP, negotiates ten kinds of options, and then carries each bridged frame or BPDU in a PPP packet with protocol type hex 0031.
tldr.outcome: This version obsoletes RFC 2878 and adds a Bridge Control Packet Indicator so that bridge control frames can get preferential treatment.

today: RFC 3518 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 2878.

sections.title: Bridging Background
sections.content:
The RFC defines the Network Control Protocol (NCP) for establishing and configuring Remote Bridging on PPP links. It starts from two bridging algorithms. Transparent Bridging keeps a forwarding database of address and interface (and VLAN ID, for bridges that support Virtual LANs). A frame with an unknown destination goes out of every interface except the one it arrived on. The Spanning Tree Protocol removes redundant paths logically, using Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs) sent from an elected Root.

Source Route Bridging, used on IEEE 802.5 Token Ring, makes the sender record the path in a Routing Information Field (RIF). Explorer frames discover paths.

PPP is used to connect Remote Bridges. For Source Route bridges the line can be modeled in two ways: as a split bridge, or as an independent-bridge LAN segment, which is the default. A device that translates between the two kinds of bridging is treated as one or the other.
sections.plainLanguage: A bridge is a helper that passes messages between two neighbourhoods. Some helpers just guess where to send things, and others write the whole route on the envelope.

sections.title: Traffic Services
sections.content:
Several services are provided for different system types. LAN Frame Checksum preservation keeps the checksum calculated by the original transmitter intact end to end, which is how an extended LAN keeps the same chance of undetected error as a single LAN. Frames with no checksum are tagged and carried across. A system that does not preserve the checksum removes the trailing four octets; one forwarding a frame without an embedded checksum onto a LAN causes it to be calculated.

Tinygram compression helps lines of 64 KBPS and below. Ethernet and IEEE 802.3 frames smaller than the minimum size are often padded with zero octets, so the sender may strip the zeros and tag the frame, and the receiver puts them back. It is the transmitter's option.

Virtual LANs keep communities apart over one line, using the VLAN ID in an IEEE 802.1Q tagged frame. The Bridge Control Packet Indicator marks packets such as Spanning Tree BPDUs and GARP PDUs, much as routing updates get IP precedence, and systems must avoid dropping or significantly delaying them.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel offers extras. It can keep the seal on each letter, squash letters that have lots of empty space, keep different clubs' mail apart, and rush the important notices.

sections.title: Running BCP over PPP
sections.content:
The Bridging Control Protocol (BCP) configures, enables and disables the bridge modules at both ends of the link. It uses the same packet exchange as LCP, with these exceptions: PPP must have reached the Network-Layer Protocol phase, a single BCP packet goes in the PPP Information field with Protocol type hex 8031, and only Codes 1 through 7 are used (Configure-Request through Code-Reject). Implementations SHOULD NOT negotiate Address-and-Control-Field-Compression or Protocol-Field-Compression except on low speed links.

Bridged traffic can flow only after BCP reaches the Opened state. Each frame or BPDU goes in one PPP packet with Protocol type hex 0031. There is no standard way to fragment bridged PDUs, so the link MUST negotiate an MRU large enough for the MAC types in use; even bridged Ethernet frames exceed the default PPP MRU of 1500 octets.

Magic Number Loopback Detection and Link-Quality-Monitoring are strongly recommended, because Spanning Tree is mostly one-way. On multiple links, a sender that cannot tell whether order matters MUST act as though all protocols need order preserved; PPP Multilink can help. A manager may inhibit BPDU exchange to split regions into separate spanning trees.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any mail goes through the tunnel, both ends must say hello and agree on the rules. After that, each parcel is wrapped in a standard wrapper marked as bridge mail.

sections.title: Bridged LAN Frame Formats
sections.content:
Each bridged frame starts with a flags and MAC type area. The flags are F (a LAN FCS is present), a reserved bit that must be zero, Z (the 802.3 pad is zero filled to minimum size) and B (bridge control packet). A 4-bit Pads field says how many pad octets to strip; padding may not exceed 15 octets. Then come the MAC Type, the destination and source MAC addresses, the LLC data and the optional LAN FCS. 802.4, 802.5 and FDDI frames also carry a pad byte and a Frame Control field.

The MAC Type values are 1 (IEEE 802.3/Ethernet, canonical addresses), 2 (802.4, canonical), 3 (802.5, non-canonical), 4 (FDDI, non-canonical), 11 (802.5, canonical) and 12 (FDDI, canonical). A system must not send a MAC Type above 4 unless the peer announced it with MAC-Support. The PPP Frame FCS is separate from the LAN FCS.

A tagged frame adds a 3-bit priority, a canonical flag and a 12-bit VLAN ID, and may be used only if the IEEE-802-Tagged-Frame option was accepted. Spanning Tree, GARP and other bridge protocol units travel in these same formats and are recognised by destination address, such as 01-80-c2-00-00-00 for the Bridge Group Address.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parcel has a small label on the front saying what kind of network it came from, plus tiny flags like 'checksum included'. Tagged parcels also say which club they belong to.

sections.title: Configuration Options
sections.content:
BCP uses LCP's option format with its own set of option types. If an option is absent from a Configure-Request, its default is assumed.

Bridge-Identification (type 1) is for lines that join two half bridges; it carries a 12-bit LAN segment number and a 4-bit bridge number, and the halves must agree on the bridge number or BCP must not open. Line-Identification (type 2) gives the line a LAN segment number, and the segment number must be agreed. A system with a mismatch may change to the higher of the two numbers but not the reverse.

MAC-Support (type 3) advises which MAC types a system will accept, and cannot be put in a Configure-Nak. Tinygram-Compression (type 4) enables (1) or disables (2) compression and defaults to none. MAC-Address (type 6) announces a MAC address, or asks for one by sending 00-00-00-00-00-00. IEEE-802-Tagged-Frame (type 8) and Management-Inline (type 9) turn on tagged frames and inline BPDU/GARP traffic. Bridge-Control-Packet-Indicator (type 10) enables the B flag; without it the bit must be 0 in every frame.
sections.plainLanguage: When the two ends say hello, each can hold up cards saying what it wants, like 'I am number 1' or 'I can read tagged parcels'. They keep talking until the cards fit together.

sections.title: Compatibility and Changes
sections.content:
This RFC obsoletes RFC 2878. Its two changes are the added Bridge Control Packet Indicator option and a changed meaning for one of the reserved flag bits. IANA assigned option value 10 for the new option.

Older implementations follow RFC 1638. The Spanning-Tree-Protocol option (type 7, old format) exists for them, and is incompatible with Management-Inline. A peer that rejects Management-Inline is taken to be an old BCP implementation, and the old BPDU format from Appendix A must then be used. A system may terminate, run without spanning tree (which the RFC calls dangerous) or fall back to compatibility mode. Implementations SHOULD implement a backward compatibility mode.

Option 5, LAN-Identification, is listed as obsoleted.
sections.plainLanguage: New tunnel rules still have to work with old tunnel ends, so there is a special old-fashioned way of talking that both can fall back on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BCP compares the configurations of two devices and negotiates an acceptable subset. A major misconfiguration stops negotiation, so the link comes down or does not come up. With a rogue peer, network information may be learned from forwarded multicast traffic, and denial of service may result from closing loops or offering rogue load.

The RFC says these attacks are common to every PPP NCP and recommends that links where this could happen use PPP authentication during LCP start-up.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger plugs into the tunnel, they could listen in or make trouble. The fix is to check who they are before letting them in.
